description: First Past the Post and proportional alternatives, and the strengths and weaknesses of each.
content_html:
Why Voting Systems Matter

The way votes are counted determines who governs. Different voting systems can produce very different outcomes from the same set of votes. The UK uses several voting systems for different elections: First Past the Post (FPTP) for Westminster general elections, and various forms of proportional representation for devolved elections and some local elections. Understanding the strengths and weaknesses of each system is a key citizenship skill.

First Past the Post (FPTP)

Under FPTP, the UK is divided into parliamentary constituencies. Each constituency elects one MP. Voters mark a cross next to their preferred candidate. The candidate with the most votes wins — they do not need a majority of votes, just more than anyone else. Westminster general elections use this system for all 650 seats.

Key Fact

Under FPTP, each constituency elects one MP — the candidate with the most votes wins, regardless of whether they have a majority. This is called a plurality. Westminster general elections take place every five years under this system.

Strengths of FPTP

Supporters of FPTP highlight several advantages. First, it usually produces a clear result: one party typically wins enough seats to form a majority government with a strong mandate to govern. Strong majority governments can implement their manifesto commitments without being blocked by coalition partners. Second, each MP represents a specific constituency, creating a direct link between voters and their elected representative. Third, the system is simple to understand and quick to count: voters mark one cross, results are declared overnight.

Supporters also argue that FPTP produces stability: governments tend to last a full term rather than collapsing when coalition partners fall out. The 2010–2015 coalition, though stable by comparative standards, showed the complexity of coalition negotiation that more proportional systems often require.

Weaknesses of FPTP

Critics of FPTP point to several serious problems. First, the system can produce large majorities from a minority of votes: a party can win a landslide majority in Parliament while winning well under half of the votes cast nationally, because votes for losing candidates in each constituency contribute nothing to the final seat count. Second, many votes are effectively “wasted” — in safe seats, the outcome is predictable regardless of the local vote, reducing the incentive to vote. Third, smaller parties that attract votes spread evenly across constituencies may win very few seats even with significant national support, meaning proportionality is low.

A very common exam error is to list FPTP advantages and disadvantages on one side, and proportional representation advantages and disadvantages on the other side, without comparing the two against each other. Examiners want explicit comparison and a substantiated judgement — for example: “While FPTP produces stable majority governments more reliably than PR, it does so at the cost of proportionality, which means millions of voters are effectively unrepresented. On balance, the gain in stability may or may not outweigh this democratic deficit depending on the criteria used.” A side-by-side list without explicit comparison and a conclusion will not reach the top band.

Proportional Representation Systems

Several forms of proportional representation (PR) are used in UK elections. These systems aim to ensure that parties win seats in rough proportion to their share of the vote, giving smaller parties and minority views better representation.

The Additional Member System (AMS) is used for elections to the Scottish Parliament and the Welsh Senedd. Voters cast two votes: one for a constituency MP (using FPTP) and one for a regional party list. The regional seats are allocated to correct for the disproportionality of the constituency results, producing an overall result closer to the share of the vote. The Scottish Parliament was designed to make single-party majority government difficult, encouraging coalition or minority government.

The Single Transferable Vote (STV) is used for Northern Ireland Assembly elections and Scottish local government elections. Voters rank candidates 1, 2, 3, and so on. Votes are transferred according to these preferences until all seats are filled. STV produces highly proportional results and gives voters more choice, but is complex to count and can produce results that are harder for voters to understand immediately.

Key Fact

The Additional Member System is used for Scottish Parliament and Welsh Senedd elections. The Single Transferable Vote is used for Northern Ireland Assembly elections. Both produce more proportional outcomes than FPTP.

Strengths and Weaknesses of PR

Supporters of proportional systems argue that they better represent the range of views in society. Smaller parties can win seats, reducing “wasted votes” and encouraging more people to vote because their vote is more likely to count. Coalitions, which PR tends to produce, can also represent a broader range of voters’ priorities.

Critics argue that PR produces weak governments: coalition partners may disagree, making it harder to implement a clear programme, and voters may not know which parties will form a government after the election. The relationship between individual voters and a specific representative can also be weakened when large multi-member constituencies replace single-member ones. There is no consensus in the UK about which system is best: this remains a contested political question on which different parties hold different positions.

In 2011, a UK-wide referendum was held on whether to replace FPTP for Westminster elections with the Alternative Vote (AV) system, in which voters rank candidates in order of preference and the lowest-placed candidate is eliminated in successive rounds until one candidate has more than half the votes. The proposal was rejected: 67.9% voted to keep FPTP and 32.1% voted for AV. The result showed that, at that point, a majority of UK voters preferred to keep the existing system. Supporters of reform argued the question was poorly framed and that AV was not a fully proportional system in any case. The debate about electoral reform continues, with supporters of more proportional systems arguing the 2011 referendum settled only the question of AV, not the broader principle of proportional representation.
exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Analyse or a 12-mark Evaluate question on voting systems, the most common error is to treat the answer as a list of pros and cons without making an explicit comparison or reaching a clear judgement. Examiners want you to weigh the arguments — for example: “FPTP produces stable majority governments, but at the cost of proportionality. The 2011 AV referendum showed that voters, at least at that time, preferred stability over greater proportionality. However, supporters of PR argue that fairness of representation matters more than ease of government formation.” Always name a real-world anchor: name a specific system (AMS, STV), name a specific election it is used for, or reference the 2011 referendum. A conclusion that merely says “both systems have advantages and disadvantages” without a judgement will not access the top band.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • First Past the Post is used for Westminster elections: the candidate with the most votes in each constituency wins the seat, which tends to produce majority governments but can produce disproportionate results.
  • Proportional systems (AMS for Scottish Parliament and Welsh Senedd; STV for Northern Ireland Assembly) give smaller parties fairer representation but can lead to coalition governments and may weaken the voter-MP link.
  • Evaluating voting systems means comparing them explicitly — choosing between stability, proportionality, simplicity and voter-representative links — rather than just listing features of each.

practice_questions.text:
Which voting system is used to elect Members of Parliament to the House of Commons at a UK general election?
A) Single Transferable Vote
B) Additional Member System
C) First Past the Post
D) Proportional Representation List
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for C) First Past the Post.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by First Past the Post.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks: 1 mark for stating that the candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins the seat; 1 mark for adding that no majority is needed — a plurality is sufficient. A one-word answer scores 0.

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of the First Past the Post voting system.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying an advantage (e.g. produces clear majority governments); 1 mark for developing the advantage with a cause-and-consequence link (e.g. because the winning party typically secures enough seats to govern alone, it can implement its manifesto without coalition compromise); 1 mark for identifying a disadvantage (e.g. many votes are wasted in safe seats and smaller parties can win few seats despite significant national support); 1 mark for developing the disadvantage with a consequence (e.g. this reduces proportionality and may reduce voter turnout in constituencies where the result seems predetermined).

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below and answer the question that follows.

"A non-partisan polling organisation surveyed 3,000 UK adults after the most recent general election. It found that 58% of respondents felt their vote had ‘made no real difference’ to the outcome, and 43% said they had voted for a party that won no seats in their constituency. The organisation concluded that under the current voting system, a significant proportion of voters feel disengaged from the electoral process."

Using the extract and your own knowledge, interpret what this source suggests about the relationship between voting systems and voter engagement.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying the key finding (majority feel their vote made no difference; many voted for losing candidates); 1 mark for interpreting what this shows (under FPTP, votes for losing candidates in each constituency do not contribute to seat allocation, leading to ‘wasted votes’); 1 mark for using own knowledge (e.g. proportional systems such as AMS or STV are designed to reduce wasted votes and give smaller parties fairer representation, potentially improving engagement); 1 mark for a substantiated judgement (e.g. the source supports the argument that FPTP contributes to voter disengagement, though the survey question about ‘feeling your vote matters’ is subjective and other factors such as candidate quality or campaign style also influence engagement).

practice_questions.text: Analyse the extent to which First Past the Post serves the needs of UK democracy better than proportional representation systems.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed two-sided analysis comparing FPTP and at least one named PR system (e.g. AMS for Scottish Parliament, STV for Northern Ireland). Named real-world anchors used on both sides (e.g. 2011 AV referendum result, devolved elections under AMS). Substantiated judgement explicitly weighs the criteria (stability vs proportionality) and reaches a clear conclusion.

Secure: Two-sided analysis with at least one named system or real reference. Both sides developed with at least one reason. Judgement present but may not be fully substantiated.

Developing: Relevant points but mainly one-sided, or both sides listed without development. Limited or no named real-world example.

Emerging: Basic points about FPTP or PR. Descriptive rather than analytical. No named system, no substantiated judgement.

practice_questions.text:
"The First Past the Post voting system should be replaced with a proportional representation system for Westminster elections."

Evaluate this statement. In your answer, consider arguments in support and arguments against, and reach a substantiated overall conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: PR systems (such as AMS and STV, used in devolved elections) produce results more closely matching vote shares, reducing ‘wasted votes’. Smaller parties and minority views gain seats, giving a wider range of voters representation. Research on devolved elections suggests voters in Scotland and Wales find multi-party politics more engaging. Coalition governments can represent a broader range of voters’ priorities.

Arguments against: FPTP typically produces majority governments with a clear mandate, avoiding the instability and post-election negotiations typical of coalition politics. The 2011 UK referendum rejected changing to AV (a related system) by 67.9% to 32.1%, suggesting voters, at that time, preferred the existing system. The direct constituency MP link — where every voter can identify their own representative — is weakened by multi-member PR constituencies. Majority governments under FPTP can implement manifesto commitments without being blocked by coalition partners.

Mastering: Balanced evaluation with named real-world examples on both sides (e.g. AMS elections to Scottish Parliament, 2011 AV referendum, FPTP producing 1997 or 2019 landslide majorities). Conclusion that goes beyond ‘both have advantages’ and makes a substantiated judgement about which criteria for judging a voting system matter most.

Secure: Two-sided argument with at least one named system or real reference. Conclusion present but may not fully justify the weighing.

Developing: Relevant points, mainly one-sided or lacking named examples. Conclusion thin.

Emerging: Basic points, largely descriptive. No named example, no substantiated conclusion.

knowledge_checks.q: Which voting system is used for elections to the Scottish Parliament?
In 2011, what was the result of the UK referendum on changing the Westminster voting system to the Alternative Vote?
options: AV was approved by 67.9% of voters
FPTP was retained; 67.9% voted against AV
The result was too close to call and a second referendum was held
AV was approved for use in Scotland only

knowledge_checks.q: Under First Past the Post, each constituency elects one MP and the candidate with the most votes — called a _____ — wins the seat.
The _____ system is used for Northern Ireland Assembly elections and allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference.
Match each voting system to the election it is used for:
right: Scottish Parliament and Welsh Senedd elections

flashcard_questions.q: What is First Past the Post (FPTP)?
flashcard_questions.a: The candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins the seat, regardless of majority.
A geographic area whose residents are represented by a single MP in the House of Commons.

flashcard_questions.q: How many parliamentary constituencies are there in the UK?
What is one key strength of FPTP?
flashcard_questions.a: Usually produces a majority government with a clear mandate and strong stability.

flashcard_questions.q: What is one key weakness of FPTP?
flashcard_questions.a: Votes for losing candidates are wasted, producing disproportionate seat allocations.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Additional Member System (AMS)?
flashcard_questions.a: A voting system combining FPTP constituency seats with regional list seats for proportionality.

flashcard_questions.q: Which two devolved parliaments use the Additional Member System?
What is the Single Transferable Vote (STV)?
flashcard_questions.a: Voters rank candidates in order; votes transfer until all seats are filled.

flashcard_questions.q: Which election uses the Single Transferable Vote in the UK?
What did the 2011 UK referendum decide about electoral reform?
flashcard_questions.a: Voters chose to keep FPTP, rejecting the Alternative Vote by 67.9% to 32.1%.

flashcard_questions.q: What does proportionality mean in the context of voting systems?
flashcard_questions.a: Parties win seats in rough proportion to their share of the national vote.

flashcard_questions.q: What type of government do proportional systems tend to produce?
flashcard_questions.a: Coalition or minority governments, requiring parties to share power.

glossary_terms.definition: A voting system in which the candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins the seat, even if they do not have more than half the total votes cast.
Geographic areas whose residents are each represented by a single MP in the House of Commons.
The fairness with which votes translate into parliamentary seats; a system is proportional when parties win seats in rough proportion to their share of the vote.
A voting system used for Scottish Parliament, Welsh Senedd and London Assembly elections, combining constituency seats with regional list seats to produce a more proportional result.
A voting system used for Northern Ireland Assembly elections in which voters rank candidates in order of preference and seats are allocated in multiple rounds until all seats are filled.
Winning more votes than any other candidate without necessarily gaining more than half the total votes cast, which is sufficient to win a seat under the First Past the Post system.
